strengths: Comprehensive empirical study evaluating 18 MLLMs across 17 misleader types on misleading visualizations, with both QA accuracy and Likert-scale consistency analyses.
Introduces and systematically compares six inference-time correction methods; identifies table-based QA and redrawing as effective, with statistical testing and analysis of trade-offs.
Combines multiple datasets (CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT, ChartQA, real-world examples) and compares model behavior to human accuracy, strengthening practical relevance.
Code and data are made available, and implementation details such as seeds and temperature are provided, supporting reproducibility.
Addresses an important reliability and safety issue for multimodal chart understanding, with clear implications for misinformation and downstream deployment.
weaknesses: The random baseline for misleading visualizations (25.6%) is not adequately explained given the mixed MCQ/free-text/rank question types; if free-text/rank questions are included, a 25.6% random baseline is implausible, potentially undermining the central claim that MLLMs fall to random performance.

The correction methods are evaluated on only three open-weight models, all of which performed below random in Experiment 1; generalization to larger or commercial models is untested, and the abstract's claim of not compromising non-misleading accuracy is contradicted by table-based QA's significant drops.
Experiment 2 uses only four visualization pairs, limiting the consistency conclusions; significant effects are found only for truncated axis, and broader misleader types are not tested.

Real-world misleading examples may be confounded by parametric knowledge (events up to 2022), which can inflate accuracy and underestimate vulnerability; the paper acknowledges this but does not fully address it experimentally.
The paper does not directly measure table extraction accuracy, so the intermediate-step analysis is indirect; dataset imbalance (e.g., some misleader categories with n=1) limits per-type claims.

Novelty is partially limited by concurrent work, and the correction methods are relatively simple prompt/extraction strategies without comparison to prior visualization linters or correction baselines.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the vulnerability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to misleading visualizations and the potential for such visualizations to spread disinformation.
Comprehensive empirical study: evaluates 18 MLLMs across multiple datasets, including a newly introduced real-world misleading visualization dataset, and analyzes performance per misleader type.
Introduces a new dataset of 42 real-world misleading visualizations with multiple-choice questions, adding a useful resource to the community.

First evaluation (to my knowledge) of six inference-time correction methods for MLLM question answering on misleading visualizations; identifies table-based QA and redrawing as effective, with valuable insights into trade-offs.
Good reproducibility: code and data are made available, and implementation details (models, prompts, random seed, temperature) are provided.
Includes human comparison from prior work and a consistency analysis (Experiment 2) that adds depth to the vulnerability assessment.
Clear presentation with informative figures; limitations are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central claim that accuracy drops to the random baseline lacks sufficient methodological detail: the paper does not clearly define how the random baseline is computed or how non-MCQ questions (free-text, rank) are scored, which weakens the comparability of this claim.

Comparisons between misleading and non-misleading datasets may be confounded by dataset differences (chart types, question difficulty, provenance); paired comparisons are limited to Experiment 2’s four pairs.
Per-misleader analysis often relies on very small samples (e.g., n=1 for some misleader categories), limiting the reliability of conclusions about specific misleader types.
The correction methods are evaluated on only three open-weight models; generalization to other MLLMs, especially commercial models, remains unclear.

The most effective correction method (table-based QA) harms accuracy on non-misleading visualizations due to table extraction errors, but the paper does not directly evaluate table extraction accuracy because ground-truth tables are unavailable, leaving a key intermediate step unquantified.
The real-world subset lacks human baseline accuracy, so the comparison between MLLMs and humans on real-world misleading visualizations is indirect.
The novelty of the proposed correction methods is modest (prompting with tables, redrawing via Matplotlib); the main contribution is empirical analysis, which may be better suited to Findings.
Experiment 2 uses only four visualization pairs, limiting statistical power and the generalizability of consistency findings.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation of 18 MLLMs across different families and sizes on misleading visualizations, providing a broad empirical snapshot of model vulnerabilities.
Introduction of a real-world misleading visualization dataset (42 instances) that complements existing synthetic benchmarks and allows testing with realistic data.
Systematic comparison of six inference-time correction methods with statistical significance testing (McNemar test), and identification of table extraction as a critical bottleneck.
Clear presentation with useful diagnostic figures, such as per-misleader accuracy (Figure 5) and correction method effects (Figure 7).
Code and data are promised to be made available, supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: The headline claim that MLLM accuracy drops to the random baseline is not rigorously established: the random baseline is not defined for all question types (free-text, rank), and the real-world subset's higher accuracy (33.5%) may be confounded by the number of answer choices (3–4 options yield a 25–33% chance level). No matched per-question random baseline is provided.
Experiment 3 evaluates correction methods on only three open-weight mid-sized models, severely limiting the generalizability of the findings about which methods are effective.

The abstract claims correction methods improve accuracy 'without compromising accuracy on non-misleading ones,' but table-based QA significantly decreases non-misleading accuracy (up to 8.5 pp). The paper later acknowledges this contradiction, but the abstract overstates the results.

The correction methods (warning, providing axes/table, table-based QA, redrawing) are straightforward prompt interventions and lack novelty; no comparison to existing approaches such as visualization linters or fine-tuning is provided.

Experiment 2 uses only four visualization pairs, which is too small to draw general conclusions about consistency across misleader types; the significance tests are underpowered and the null results for some misleaders are not informative.
The manually created real-world dataset (n=42) lacks reported annotation guidelines, inter-annotator agreement, or validation of question quality, limiting reproducibility and reliability.
Potential confounds are not controlled: datasets differ in question types, number of answer choices, and difficulty, making cross-dataset comparisons and human–model comparisons problematic.
The paper's methodological contribution to NLP is limited; it is primarily an empirical visualization study and may be better suited to a visualization venue (e.g., IEEE VIS, CHI) than ACL.
The paper identifies table extraction as a key bottleneck but offers no error analysis or proposed improvements, leaving a critical component unaddressed.

The evaluation focuses on QA accuracy and Likert consistency but does not measure whether corrections actually reduce the misleading effect (e.g., whether models become less susceptible to distorted data) or introduce new biases.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical scope: the paper evaluates 19 MLLMs (11 open-weight, 5 commercial, 3 chart-specialized) across three datasets plus a newly introduced real-world subset, which is substantially broader than prior work on this problem.

Practical, well-motivated contribution: the comparison of six inference-time correction methods, and in particular the explicit trade-off analysis between improving accuracy on misleading visualizations and preserving accuracy on non-misleading ones, is a genuinely useful contribution that prior work did not address.

Clear and actionable findings: table-based QA and redrawing the visualization yield significant improvements (up to 19.6 pp) while a set of other methods (warning, axes, axes+table) are shown to be ineffective, with the paper diagnosing why (e.g., MLLMs ignore tabular/axes side-information and stay biased toward the image).

Good reproducibility practices: code and data released under CC-BY-SA-4.0, full prompts provided in appendices, temperature fixed to 0, and statistical tests (paired t-test, McNemar) reported with p-values.

Careful failure-mode analysis: the manual analysis of table/axes extraction errors (Appendices H and I, Tables 4-6) and the qualitative examples (Figures 13-15) provide mechanistic insight into why table-based QA succeeds or fails per misleader type.
Thoughtful discussion of human-vs-MLLM differences (e.g., area encoding and dual axis), which helps motivate why methods designed to protect humans may not transfer to MLLMs.
Honest limitations section and clear positioning against concurrent work.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central vulnerability claim: parallel and prior work (Bendeck & Stasko 2025; Chen et al. 2025; Pandey & Ottley 2025; Valentim et al. 2025) has already documented MLLM susceptibility to misleading visualizations, so the main novel increment is the correction-method comparison rather than the discovery of the vulnerability.

Small and imbalanced datasets: the misleading dataset has only n=143 instances and the non-misleading n=124, with several misleader categories represented by a single example (inappropriate pie chart, missing data, overplotting) and only 42 real-world instances. Per-misleader conclusions therefore rest on very thin evidence, and the paper acknowledges this imbalance.

Experiment 2 (consistency) is based on only four visualization pairs, two of which show non-significant differences; the evidence for the consistency claim is correspondingly weak and the generalizability is unclear.

Correction methods are only evaluated on three mid-sized open-weight models (Qwen2VL-7B, Ovis1.6-9B, InternVL2.5-8B), all of which underperform the random baseline in Experiment 1; it is unclear whether the conclusions transfer to stronger models (e.g., GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-sonnet) that already perform better on misleading visualizations.

The misleader-warning method relies on ground-truth misleader labels, making it an unrealistic upper bound; the paper acknowledges this but still frames the result as an effectiveness comparison, which may overstate practical viability.

The claim that strong models' advantage on the real-world subset stems from parametric knowledge is partly speculative, though Appendix C offers a partial (n=22) self-contained-question check; the parametric-knowledge confound also means the real-world subset may not cleanly measure visual robustness.

Redrawing via default Matplotlib settings is a somewhat crude correction and the reported gains depend on code compiling successfully (success rates as low as 79% for scatter plots); the method's robustness across chart types is not fully characterized.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important reliability/safety problem: MLLMs are vulnerable to misleading visualizations, which has direct implications for misinformation and real-world chart understanding.

Broad empirical scope: evaluates 19 MLLMs across multiple datasets (CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT, ChartQA, and a newly annotated real-world set), 17 misleader types, and both QA accuracy and Likert-scale consistency.

Provides a useful comparison of six inference-time correction methods, with statistical testing and qualitative error analyses, showing that table-based QA and redrawing can substantially improve accuracy on misleading visualizations.
Clear presentation, informative figures, and extensive appendix material including prompts, misleader definitions, and extraction error analyses; code and data are promised for release.

Carefully documents trade-offs: table-based QA can improve misleading-chart accuracy but may degrade non-misleading performance, and redrawing is model-dependent, which is valuable nuance for future work.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited relative to concurrent/parallel work that also documents MLLM vulnerability to misleading visualizations; the paper's main addition is breadth and a correction-method comparison rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

The correction methods are evaluated only on three open-weight MLLMs, not on the full set of 19 or on the strongest proprietary models (GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude), so claims about general effectiveness are not fully supported.

Datasets are small and imbalanced: the misleading set has n=143, the non-misleading set n=124, several misleader categories have very few instances (some n=1), and the consistency experiment uses only four visualization pairs, limiting statistical power and per-misleader conclusions.

Table-based QA and redrawing depend on intermediate table extraction, which is shown to fail for important misleaders such as dual axis, inverted axis, and 3D effects; improvements are therefore conditional and come with non-trivial degradations on non-misleading data.

The real-world subset is potentially confounded by parametric knowledge: GPT-4o can answer many rephrased MCQs without the image (50%), which may inflate apparent robustness and complicate interpretation of the real-world results.

Statistical rigor could be improved: multiple comparisons across many models and misleader types are not corrected, and human comparisons rely on prior reported numbers rather than a controlled human study on the same stimuli.
Reproducibility is only partial because several evaluated models are proprietary APIs and may change over time, although open-weight models, prompts, and planned code/data release help.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: the robustness of multimodal large language models to misleading visualizations, with clear relevance to NLP/CL and multimodal misinformation.
Broad empirical scope: evaluates 19 MLLMs across multiple datasets (CALVI, CHARTOM, VLAT, ChartQA, and a new real-world set) and 17 misleader types.
Three complementary experiments examine QA accuracy, Likert-scale consistency, and six inference-time correction methods, yielding useful per-model and per-misleader analyses.

Provides concrete practical findings: warning messages, axes prompting, and table prompting are largely ineffective; table-based QA and visualization redrawing can improve misleading-chart QA; table extraction is a key bottleneck.
Good reproducibility intentions: releases code/data under open licenses, includes prompts, implementation details, and appendix error analyses.
Honest limitations section and nuanced discussion of human-vs-MLLM differences (e.g., area encoding, dual axis) add value.
Identifies an important design principle: removing or modifying the misleading visualization is more effective than merely supplementing the prompt with additional extracted information.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction claim correction methods improve misleading-chart QA "without compromising accuracy on non-misleading ones," but Experiment 3 shows table-based QA significantly degrades non-misleading accuracy for two models (up to 8.5 pp), directly contradicting the framing.

The real-world subset is confounded by parametric knowledge: many questions are answerable without the image (e.g., GPT-4o gets 50% without the visualization), so higher accuracy on this subset may not reflect visual robustness and contaminates the overall vulnerability estimate.
Experiment 2 is thin: only four visualization pairs, with significant inconsistency only for truncated-axis pairs; conclusions about broader misleader consistency are weak and heavily hedged.
The correction-method evaluation uses only three open-weight mid-sized MLLMs, not the full 19-model set or strong commercial models, limiting generalizability of the mitigation claims.

Limited technical novelty: the paper compares existing inference-time prompting methods rather than proposing a new correction method; the contribution is largely empirical and incremental relative to prior chart-QA and parallel vulnerability work.

Table-based QA depends on imperfect table extraction (0% for dual axis, 8.3% for 3D effects, etc.), and redrawing depends on successful code compilation; practical reliability and end-to-end integration are not established.

Statistical rigor is uneven: Experiment 1 lacks significance tests or confidence intervals; Experiment 2 uses one-sided paired t-tests without clear directional justification and without multiple-comparison correction; the random-baseline computation is not fully specified.
Dataset limitations remain: small size, imbalanced misleader categories, and manually created real-world MCQs without reported inter-annotator agreement, which may introduce annotation artifacts.

The "first comprehensive study/first comparison" claim is not fully substantiated given parallel work (Bendeck & Stasko, 2025; Pandey & Ottley, 2025; Chen et al., 2025) and existing chart-QA literature.
Some vulnerability estimates rely on comparisons to ChartQA that are not distribution-matched, which may overstate the drop in MLLM performance on misleading charts.

Practical deployment concerns are underexplored: the warning method assumes ground-truth misleader labels, no misleader detector is evaluated, and the correction methods are not tested in an end-to-end system.
